{{Too technical|date=February 2025}}
{{Short description|Type of elliptic curve}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Montgomery curve''' is a form of [[elliptic curve]] introduced by [[Peter Montgomery (mathematician)|Peter L. Montgomery]] in 1987,<ref>{{cite journal
 | author = [[Peter Montgomery (mathematician)|Peter L. Montgomery]]
 | year = 1987
 | title = Speeding the Pollard and Elliptic Curve Methods of Factorization
 | journal = Mathematics of Computation |volume=48 |issue=177 |pages=243–264
 | jstor = 2007888
 | doi=10.2307/2007888
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref> different from the usual [[Weierstrass form]]. It is used for certain computations, and in particular in different [[Elliptic curve cryptography|cryptography]] applications.

==Definition==
[[File:Montgomery curve2.svg|300px|right|thumb|A Montgomery curve of equation <math display="inline">\frac{1}{4}y^2=x^3+\frac{5}{2}x^2+x</math>]]
A Montgomery curve over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] {{math|''K''}} is defined by the [[equation]]

:<math>M_{A,B}: By^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 + x</math>

for {{math|''A'', ''B'' ∈ ''K''}} such that {{math|''B''(''A''<sup>2</sup> − 4) ≠ 0}}.

Generally this [[curve]] is considered over a [[finite field]] ''K'' (for example, over a finite field of {{math|''q''}} [[element (mathematics)|element]]s, {{math|1=''K'' = '''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>}}) with [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] different from 2 and with {{math|''A'' ≠ ±2}} and {{math|''B'' ≠ 0}}. Over such fields, the group order of the curve is always divisible by 4. Montgomery curves are also considered over the [[rational number|rationals]] with the same restrictions for {{math|''A''}} and {{math|''B''}}.

Every Montgomery curve has a point at <math>(0,0)</math>.

==Montgomery arithmetic==
It is possible to do some "operations" between the [[point (geometry)|points]] of an elliptic curve:  "adding" two points <math>P, Q</math> consists of finding a third one <math>R</math> such that <math>R=P+Q</math>; "doubling" a point consists of computing <math>[2]P=P+P</math> (For more information about operations see [[Elliptic curve#The group law|The group law]]) and below.

A point <math>P=(x,y)</math> on the elliptic curve in the Montgomery form <math>By^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 + x</math> can be represented in Montgomery coordinates <math>P=(X:Z)</math>, where <math>P=(X:Z)</math> are [[projective space|projective coordinates]] and <math>x=X/Z</math> for <math>Z\ne 0</math>.

Notice that this kind of representation for a point loses information: indeed, in this case, there is no distinction between the [[affine space|affine points]] <math>(x,y)</math> and <math>(x,-y)</math> because they are both given by the point <math>(X:Z)</math>. However, with this representation it is possible to obtain multiples of points, that is, given <math>P=(X:Z)</math>, to compute <math>[n]P=(X_n:Z_n)</math>.

Now, considering the two points <math>P_n=[n]P=(X_n:Z_n)</math> and <math>P_m=[m]P=(X_m:Z_m)</math>: their [[summation|sum]] is given by the point <math>P_{m+n}=P_m+P_n = (X_{m+n}:Z_{m+n})</math> whose [[coordinate system|coordinates]] are:

: <math>
X_{m+n} = Z_{m-n}((X_m-Z_m)(X_n+Z_n)+(X_m+Z_m)(X_n-Z_n))^2
</math>

: <math>
Z_{m+n} = X_{m-n}((X_m-Z_m)(X_n+Z_n)-(X_m+Z_m)(X_n-Z_n))^2
</math>

If <math>m=n</math>, then the operation becomes a "doubling"; the coordinates of <math>[2]P_n=P_n+P_n=P_{2n}=(X_{2n}:Z_{2n})</math> are given by the following equations:

: <math>
4X_nZ_n = (X_n+Z_n)^2 - (X_n-Z_n)^2
</math>

: <math>
X_{2n} = (X_n+Z_n)^2(X_n-Z_n)^2
</math>

: <math>
Z_{2n} = (4X_nZ_n)((X_n-Z_n)^2+((A+2)/4)(4X_nZ_n))
</math>

The first operation considered above ([[elliptic curve#The group law|addition]]) has a time-cost of 3'''M'''+2'''S''', where '''M''' denotes the multiplication between two general [[element (mathematics)|elements]] of the field on which the elliptic curve is defined, while '''S''' denotes [[square (algebra)|squaring]] of a general element of the field.

The second operation (doubling) has a time-cost of 2'''M'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2'''S'''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1'''D''', where '''D''' denotes the multiplication of a general element by a [[constant (mathematics)|constant]]; notice that the constant is <math>(A+2)/4</math>, so <math>A</math> can be chosen in order to have a small&nbsp;'''D'''.

==Algorithm and example==
The following algorithm represents a doubling of a point <math>P_1=(X_1:Z_1)</math> on an elliptic curve in the Montgomery form.

It is assumed that <math>Z_1=1</math>. The cost of this implementation is 1M + 2S + 1*A + 3add + 1*4. Here M denotes the multiplications required, S indicates the squarings, and a refers to the multiplication by A.

: <math>XX_1 = X_1^2 \, </math>

: <math>X_2 = (XX_1-1)^2 \, </math>

: <math>Z_2 = 4X_1(XX_1+aX_1+1) \, </math>

===Example===
Let <math>P_1=(2,\sqrt{3})</math> be a point on the curve <math>2y^2 = x^3 -x^2 + x</math>.
In coordinates <math>(X_1:Z_1)</math>, with <math>x_1=X_1/Z_1</math>, <math>P_1=(2:1)</math>.

Then:

: <math>XX_1 = X_1^2 = 4 \, </math>

: <math>X_2 = (XX_1-1)^2 = 9 \, </math>

: <math>Z_2 = 4X_1(XX_1+AX_1+1) = 24 \, </math>

The result is the point <math>P_2=(X_2:Z_2)=(9:24)</math> such that <math>P_2=2P_1</math>.

==Addition==
Given two points <math>P_1=(x_1,y_1)</math>, <math>P_2=(x_2,y_2)</math> on the Montgomery curve <math>M_{A,B}</math> in affine coordinates, the point <math>P_3=P_1+P_2</math> represents, [[geometry|geometrically]] the third point of intersection between <math>M_{A,B}</math> and the line passing through <math>P_1</math> and <math>P_2</math>. It is possible to find the coordinates <math>(x_3,y_3)</math> of <math>P_3</math>, in the following way:

1) consider a generic line <math>~y=lx+m</math> in the affine plane and let it pass through <math>P_1</math> and <math>P_2</math> (impose the condition), in this way, one obtains <math>l=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}</math> and <math>m=y_1-\left(\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\right)x_1</math>;

2) intersect the line with the curve <math>M_{A,B}</math>, substituting the <math>~y</math> variable in the curve equation with <math>~y=lx+m</math>; the following [[equation| equation of third degree]] is obtained:

: <math>x^3+(A-Bl^2)x^2+(1-2Blm)x-Bm^2=0.</math>

As it has been observed before, this equation has three solutions that correspond to the <math>~x</math> coordinates of <math>P_1</math>, <math>P_2</math> and <math>P_3</math>. In particular this equation can be re-written as:

: <math>(x-x_1)(x-x_2)(x-x_3)=0</math>

3) Comparing the coefficients of the two identical equations given above, in particular the coefficients of the terms of second degree, one gets:

: <math>-x_1-x_2-x_3=A-Bl^2</math>.

So, <math>x_3</math> can be written in terms of <math>x_1</math>, <math>y_1</math>, <math>x_2</math>, <math>y_2</math>, as:

: <math>x_3 = B\left(\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\right)^2-A-x_1-x_2.</math>

4) To find the <math>~y</math> coordinate of the point <math>P_3</math> it is sufficient to substitute the value <math>x_3</math> in the line <math>~y=lx+m</math>. Notice that this will not give the point <math>P_3</math> directly. Indeed, with this method one find the coordinates of the point <math>~R</math> such that <math>R+P_1+P_2=P_\infty</math>, but if one needs the resulting point of the sum between <math>P_1</math> and <math>P_2</math>, then it is necessary to observe that: <math>R+P_1+P_2=P_\infty</math> [[if and only if]] <math>-R=P_1+P_2</math>. So, given the point <math>~R</math>, it is necessary to find <math>~-R</math>, but this can be done easily by changing the sign to the <math>~y</math> coordinate of <math>~R</math>. In other words, it will be necessary to change the sign of the <math>~y</math> coordinate obtained by substituting the value <math>x_3</math> in the equation of the line.

Resuming, the coordinates of the point <math>P_3=(x_3,y_3)</math>, <math>P_3=P_1+P_2</math> are:

: <math>x_3 = \frac{B(y_2-y_1)^2}{(x_2-x_1)^2}-A-x_1-x_2</math>

: <math>y_3 = \frac{(2x_1+x_2+A)(y_2-y_1)}{x_2-x_1}-\frac{B(y_2-y_1)^3}{(x_2-x_1)^3}-y_1</math>

==Doubling==
Given a point <math>P_1</math> on the Montgomery curve <math>M_{A,B}</math>, the point <math>[2]P_1</math> represents geometrically the third point of intersection between the curve and the line tangent to <math>P_1</math>; so, to find the coordinates of the point <math>P_3=2P_1</math> it is sufficient to follow the same method given in the addition formula; however, in this case, the line ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''lx''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''m'' has to be tangent to the curve at <math>P_1</math>, so, if <math>M_{A,B}: f(x,y)=0</math> with

: <math>f(x,y)=x^3+Ax^2+x-By^2,</math>

then the value of ''l'', which represents the [[slope]] of the line, is given by:

: <math> l=-\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right/\frac{\partial f}{\partial y }</math>

by the [[implicit function theorem]].

So <math>l = \frac{3x_1^2 + 2Ax_1 + 1}{2By_1}</math> and the coordinates of the point <math>P_3</math>, <math>P_3=2P_1</math> are:

: <math>
\begin{align}
x_3 & = Bl^2-A-x_1-x_1 = \frac{B(3x_1^2+2Ax_1+1)^2}{(2By_1)^2}-A-x_1-x_1 \\
y_3 & = (2x_1+x_1+A)l-Bl^3-y_1 \\
& = \frac{(2x_1+x_1+A)(3{x_1}^2+2Ax_1+1)}{2By_1}-\frac{B(3{x_1}^2+2Ax_1+1)^3}{(2By_1)^3}-y_1.
\end{align}
</math>

==Equivalence with twisted Edwards curves==
Let <math>K</math> be a field with characteristic different from 2.

Let <math>M_{A,B}</math> be an elliptic curve in the Montgomery form:

: <math>M_{A,B} : Bv^2 = u^3 + Au^2 + u</math>

with <math>A\in K\smallsetminus\{-2,2\}</math>, <math>B \in K\smallsetminus\{0\}</math>

and let <math>E_{a,d}</math> be an elliptic curve in the twisted Edwards form:

: <math>E_{a,d}\  :\  ax^2 + y^2 = 1 + dx^2y^2, \,</math>

with <math>a,d\in K\smallsetminus\{0\}, \quad a\neq d.</math>

The following theorem shows the [[Birational geometry|birational equivalence]] between Montgomery curves and [[twisted Edwards curve]]:<ref>{{cite book
 | author = [[Daniel J. Bernstein]], Peter Birkner, Marc Joye, [[Tanja Lange]] and Christiane Peters
 | title = Progress in Cryptology – AFRICACRYPT 2008
 | volume = 5023
 | pages = 389–405
 | year = 2008
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg
 | isbn = 978-3-540-68159-5
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-68164-9_26
 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science
 | chapter = Twisted Edwards Curves
 | chapter-url = http://eprint.iacr.org/2008/013
 }}</ref>

'''Theorem''' (i) Every twisted Edwards curve is birationally equivalent to a Montgomery curve over <math>K</math>.
In particular, the twisted Edwards curve <math>E_{a,d}</math> is birationally equivalent to the Montgomery curve <math>M_{A,B}</math> where <math>A = \frac{2(a+d)}{a-d}</math>, and <math>B = \frac{4}{a-d}</math>.

The [[map (mathematics)|map]]:

: <math>\psi\,:\,E_{a,d} \rightarrow M_{A,B}</math>

: <math>
(x,y) \mapsto (u,v) = \left(\frac{1+y}{1-y},\frac{1+y}{(1-y)x}\right)
</math>

is a birational equivalence from <math>E_{a,d}</math> to <math>M_{A,B}</math>, with inverse:

: <math>\psi^{-1}</math>: <math>M_{A,B} \rightarrow E_{a,d}</math>

: <math>
(u,v) \mapsto (x,y) = \left(\frac{u}{v},\frac{u-1}{u+1}\right),
a=\frac{A+2}{B}, d=\frac{A-2}{B}
</math>

Notice that this equivalence between the two curves is not valid everywhere: indeed the map <math>\psi</math> is not defined at the points <math>v = 0</math> or <math>u + 1 = 0</math> of the <math>M_{A,B}</math>.

==Equivalence with Weierstrass curves==
Any elliptic curve can be written in Weierstrass form. In particular, the elliptic curve in the Montgomery form

: <math>M_{A,B}</math>:  <math>By^2 = x^3 + Ax^2 + x,</math>

can be transformed in the following way:
divide each term of the equation for <math>M_{A,B}</math> by <math>B^3</math>, and substitute the variables ''x'' and ''y'', with <math>u=\frac{x}{B}</math> and <math>v=\frac{y}{B}</math> respectively, to get the equation

: <math>v^2 = u^3 + \frac{A}{B}u^2 + \frac{1}{B^2}u. </math>

To obtain a short Weierstrass form from here, it is sufficient to replace ''u'' with the variable <math>t-\frac{A}{3B}</math>:

: <math>v^2 = \left(t-\frac{A}{3B}\right)^3 + \frac{A}{B}\left(t-\frac{A}{3B}\right)^2 + \frac{1}{B^2}\left(t-\frac{A}{3B}\right); </math>

finally, this gives the equation:

: <math>v^2 = t^3 + \left(\frac{3-A^2}{3B^2}\right)t + \left(\frac{2A^3-9A}{27B^3}\right).
 </math>

Hence the mapping is given as

: <math>\psi</math>: <math>M_{A,B} \rightarrow E_{a,b}</math>

: <math>
(x,y) \mapsto (t,v) = \left(\frac{x}{B} + \frac{A}{3B}, \frac{y}{B}\right),
a=\frac{3-A^2}{3B^2}, b=\frac{2A^3-9A}{27B^3}
</math>

In contrast, an elliptic curve over base field <math>\mathbb{F}</math> in Weierstrass form

: <math>E_{a,b}</math>: <math>v^2 = t^3 + at + b</math>

can be converted to Montgomery form if and only if <math>E_{a,b}</math> satisfies the following conditions:<ref>{{cite conference
| author = Katsuyuki Okeya, Hiroyuki Kurumatani, and Kouichi Sakurai
| year = 2000
| title = Elliptic Curves with the Montgomery-Form and Their Cryptographic Applications
| conference = Public Key Cryptography (PKC2000)
| doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-46588-1_17
| doi-access = free
}}</ref>

# <math>z^3 + az + b = 0</math> has at least one root <math>\alpha \in \mathbb{F}</math>; and
# <math>3\alpha^2 + a</math> is a [[quadratic residue]] in <math>\mathbb{F}</math>.

When these conditions are satisfied, then for <math>s = (\sqrt{3\alpha^2 + a})^{-1}</math> we have the mapping

: <math>\psi^{-1}</math>: <math>E_{a,b} \rightarrow M_{A,B}</math>

: <math>
(t,v) \mapsto (x,y) =
\left(s (t-\alpha), s v\right),
A = 3 \alpha s,
B = s
</math>.
